title: An alternative approach to digital sovereignty: Confidential Computing

segments.text: Thank you very much indeed. It's lovely to be here in Berlin um again. Uh and so I'm here to talk about uh digital sovereignty and confidential computing
obviously. Um and I don't think that AI is very good at doing developer um uh slides yet. So apologies if they're not what you want.
Um but I really do want you to be asking questions. So I'm going to try and get through them fairly quickly. give you the the main idea of what I'm talking
about so that you can ask questions. Um I am the uh executive director of the confidential computer consortium which is like a trade body around confidential
computing. We're part of the Linux Foundation. So we're also very big into open source. Um so let's first talk about what we mean by by sovereignty.
Um, and when we think of sovereignty, we tend to think about national digital sovereignty. There's a lot of work going in the EU, in Japan, in India, in
individual EU states about protecting uh the data of its citizens and businesses from people who shouldn't have it. Uh, and that can mean anything from other
organizations all the way up to governments who shouldn't have access to it. But I think also we should be thinking about organizational sovereignty. Organizations want to be
able to look after that data and personal sovereignty in that people, individuals want to make sure that their data is correctly used and correctly
managed. And the illusion is that we can do all of this just with contracts uh and just with I promise to do the right thing. you go to your CSP and they
uh they will definitely not look in and they will definitely not look in even if a government tells them to look in. Of course, there's issues with hackers
or crackers uh and other folks as well, but if we're relying on contractual information uh contractual agreements and the data just being in what you hope
is the right place, that's not enough. We are we're technologists, right? Developers, architects, and we want to be using technological and stronger technological uh asurances than just
contracts on paper. So where we really want to be is to be able to isolate that data and applications and AI models and agents
and all of those things at a at a technical level using preferably hardware and cryptography to keep things as safe as possible. We want to move from sovereignty being
this legal checkbox idea where say oh yes we'll keep it safe to a cryptographic hardwarebacked guarantee. The other thing of course is that compliance is really important. Who who
here loves auditors? It's really weird no one puts their hands up when I ask that question. I I have been an auditor in my past. I'm
over it now. I admit it. Uh I've gone through the 12 this 12step plan. Um, but auditors are important because they report to regulators and they report to
the boards and the CISOs and the CFOs and they need to be able to prove to those people that the protections in place are sufficient and if it's just
paper that is not sufficient in this day and age, particularly as things move so quickly and we have AI being able to uh find vulnerabil abilities exfiltrate
data much more quickly than humans are able typically to defend against it. So how do we think about this? Well, please tell please tell me that everyone here
already uses encryption for data at rest. Nod. Nod. Yes. Okay. Hands up. That's good. Please. I' I'd like a few more hands than that, but that that's
that's okay. Good. Please tell me also that you use encryption for data in transit, right? TLS, ipseack, all of the Yes. Okay. This is a good you you know
this, right? The problem is that there's another state in which data exists and that is when it's in use, when it's in RAM, when it's being accessed, when it's
being used for things, and when it's there, it is not protected. The way that modern virtualization works is that if you have access to the kernel
or the hypervisor or admin access, you get to see all of that data. It is stored on that machine as it's being used. You can look at it because that's
how virtualization works and containers work. And that is a problem because it's exposed anyone who does have access to that can absolutely look at it.
So we want to move from this old idea of administrative controls to a uh a cryptographic and hardwarebased protection mechanism and that is what
confidential computing provides. Before I go on, I should say that confidential computing is available on all the major cloud providers now, both in the US and Europe and elsewhere in
the world. It's available in CPUs. It's available in GPUs from Nvidia and others coming. It's available in hardware you can buy off the shelf right now. Now in
AMD uh chips and Intel chips and ARM chips coming and other places as well. It is absolutely there. If you're not using it, it's because you haven't heard
of it or don't realize how important it is that you should be using it. And what confidential computing does is it creates what we call a trusted
execution environment. And it's it's basically a set of memory pages, right? A set of memory pages which are encrypted in RAM. The exact mechanism
used depends on the architecture but they are isolated from the rest of the machine which means that even if you do have hypervisor access or admin access
or kernel access you cannot look at the uh those memory pages in clear and you cannot change them. We have integrity and confidentiality protections.
They are only ever decrypted or accessed when they're on the CPU or on the GPU. So you need physical attacks actually to get at them.
So this is what I mean by hardwarebased protections. These are uh mechanisms which protect and isolate that data whilst it's in use. And it can be used
you can be executing processes within a trusted execution environment. And the one of the big use cases at the moment is looking at uh aentic AI for instance
where you may worry that you know you've got stuff on an MCP server or on a client and you've got credit card details or personal details or um uh
instructions about what stock to sell or what databases you're scraping. Being able to protect that from whoever has access to the rest of the
infrastructure gives you a huge improvement in what's going on. So these are absolutely processes that you can run and I'll talk about a couple more
examples later on. So what we're saying is that if we're using trust execution environments, we should be protected against all of these people who in most cases you do
not want to have access to your data. You might need a cloud CIS admin to have access to your control plane, but you almost certainly don't want to have them
to have access to your data plane and the data in use. Ditto your partners who are providing IT support, your lovely banks and enterprises and
definitely not external or let's be face it internal hackers because we can also protect of course against insider threats. And so this is what confidential
computing provides. It provides isolation from these different uh uh entities who shouldn't have unauthorized access. It provides confidentiality basically via encryption so that no one
can look in and if they exfiltrate anything it's means nothing at all and integrity. So you not only know that the stuff is protected but also uh from
being being seen but also it can't be changed. And that's really important because you may want to be able to say I want to check that the uh the output of
this program this application is what I think it is because because it is the application that I loaded in the first place. No one could have changed it.
Right? But there's another thing as well which is really important. And this is remote attestation. And remote attestation allows you to say you know what I can prove that what is
in that trusted execution environment that TE that confidential computing environment is what I think it is. Because what happens is when you add your uh application and your data sets
or your uh data models or whatever it may be your AI models, you can ask the system to measure what they are hash what that
is. sign it again at the hardware layer and then pass that to a trusted third party or do it yourself and check that what is
there is what you think was in there and what you intended to be loading or you can use that proof to other people say look this is what I say is in
here you can trust it because look it's open source you've you hashed it yourself you know what it looked like and so that could go all the way across
to to the developer developer you can be sure but also to folks like auditors who we've already discussed we love so much but we need to be keeping on site.
So we've got something which is a receipt of what's going on which we can say this is what happened. This is what's in here. We're now happy to
proceed. Again, this actually allows us to do a whole bunch of really interesting things beyond just uh data sovereignty and digital sovereignty and I'll come on to
a few of those things. But it does allow us to be doing uh these sovereignty things because we can say I am only putting information in here
that is the right data. I am proving via the application that I can never exfiltrate it or it can never go in the wrong place and I can also
prove that it is protected from other people looking in because it is in a trusted execution environment from one of these hardware providers who I trust.
So this is kind of the the change. This is where we want to be going and this is what I want you to be thinking about as
you leave uh this conference and go back to your places of work. When we're doing traditional cloud security, we have to rely on software
policies. We can only do data protection at rest and in transit. And when it comes to it, the people I trust or the things I trust
have to be the cloud provider and the host OS because if either of them do something wrong, it's all gone. I can't trust any
of this stuff at all. I can't be sure it's not been tampered and changed and I can't be sure it's not been exfiltrated. And when I try to create a proof to show
my auditor, it'd say look uh we we create a long document with you know 50,000 pages or 1,400 pages or whatever and say it's good. It must be good right
that is not good enough. What we want to go to is this other option. This is I mean not the only way of doing it but
it's a very performant and easy to use way of doing it which is confidential computing where we have silicon level hardware isolation based on these
trusted execution environments. It's encrypted in use which is in green and really important because somehow my AI slide creator decided it was important. It's it's fair. The root of trust is no
longer the host OS or the cloud provider. It's the CPU. Now, you always have to trust your CPU anyway, right? Because it's doing the execution.
So, you have to trust something, something we call sometimes the bottom turtle. There's got to be something at the bottom that we trust. Um
and the compliance proof which we use ourselves or or give to regulators or whatever it may be is a cryptographic signature based in uh based on things
provided by the hardware. Now I said a little earlier on uh that when you create this uh uh it's called attestation report you probably give it to a third party
attistation service. Let me explain why. So if let's say you're using a cloud provider and you get them to say this is correct. Well, we've got a bit of a
problem because we're trying not to trust the cloud provider, right? It's like they're marking their own homework. Have you set this up correctly so that
you can't look in? Oh yes, of course I have. You can trust me. Now, most of the time, of course, they will, but you
can't have that level of assurance. Um, it may be that uh that you are you can do the attestation checking yourself, but it's a complex thing. It
requires you to know what's going on and to get it exactly right. Cryptography, believe me, is a complex set of operations. And so it may be you want to
have an external trusted party doing that. So we need to think about that as well. So where do we get to when we're talking
about uh uh about digital sovereignty, particularly national sovereignty? Well, typically um you will have in this sort of case a depending on the the sector
maybe banking, maybe healthcare, maybe government. you'll have a local uh uh custodian who looks after uh cryptographic keys and they will be the one that interacts with um the the
hardwarebased TE and here's the important bit that TE does not need to be in the country which is provide which needs that sovereignty right so it may be depending
on everyone's risk factors etc that you are happy being in Germany for your data to be processed in Ireland or the US as long as you can prove that you're using
confidential computing throughout. Case in point, I was speaking to some folks from Japan recently. They don't have very many um they don't have enough GPUs out there at
the moment. And if they want to use AI and GPUs, they really need to do it in the states, but they need they're concerned about that. So they can they
are using confidential computing to uh protect their models and what they're doing. So what I want to go on just to finish off quickly is to say this isn't just a
uh a fix for one problem. It allows us to do a whole bunch of new and interesting things. And uh I've got three examples for you. So the first one
is a is a confidential clean room, right? Where you want to be uh processing uh data from let's say a couple of banks uh and getting
information out of it. But the bank doesn't want you to have all of their data or your AI to have all of your data. um and uh also the other bank
doesn't want to share to to sort of mix their data. But if you can prove to them that the uh that the processing is going
to take place in a a protected isolated uh environment where that data can never get fully ex exfiltrated only the results can and where we're deleted as
soon as it's done suddenly they may become interested there may be opportunities to work with them after all. So the next one is uh digital supply
chains. When you build uh your Sbomb or your AI bomb or your C bomb, it's all very well saying it built correctly using the stuff that I I think
it should be built with. But unless you've built that on a machine that you fully trust, you built from the ground up with an OS that you're fully happy
with, you cannot be sure that it's been hasn't been compromised. This could easily have happened if you're building on the cloud, for instance. If you want
to be able to have a provenence chain uh back all the way through the different pieces that are built, then building them in trusted execution
